doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Playing every style, Keith Richards, and learning from others
summary: Pallo explains how he moves from Keith Richards to Tony Bennett; sixteen standards CDs with Richards and a chord Richards showed him.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I can tell by the people you’ve played with that you don’t discount much music that I can see, that you’re prepared to play almost every kind of music that comes along.
How did that happen? How do you prepare?
As far as if I’m going to do a job that is out of my range?
Well you’ve gone from Keith Richards to Tony Bennett. So —

Well okay, all right, well it’s basically the same except of course like Keith, that’s another story, he is a great rock & roll player. A great rock & roll player. And when we get together I’ll do my thing, he does his thing, and we usually do everything live and like in a circle, live microphones and I’ll play my way of playing, he plays his way and it just sort of blends. It sort of really blends. Of course sometimes maybe I have to change a little bit if you’re going to do a rock type thing. But most of the things I do with Keith are standards. We did a lot of standards. We did 16 CDs and I have them all home, of [sings]

I wonder who’s kissing her now — songs like this. This is Keith Richards. We did “Over the Rainbow,” “Nearness of You,” songs like that. And he’s learning from me and I’m learning from him. I’m actually learning from him too. And he’s the first one that said here’s a chord that you don’t know. And he played it and I have it on CD where he is saying “I’ve got one Lou Pallo doesn’t know.” It’s funny. And I’m looking at him and saying, “I know it.” And he says, “No, you don’t know this one.” But it’s cute though. It was just a triad.
It was a G B D let’s say, it was a G B D but the way he put it, the way he formed it, I just don’t play that version. But when I played it I looked at him and I said “hmm.” And now I use it.
I do use it once in a while. That’s what we were just talking about, you learn from other people.
